title: Gases and kinetic theory
summary: Learn how pressure and temperature come from moving particles.
olay.h: Why were the specks in water shaking?
olay.p: Botanist Robert Brown watched tiny specks released from pollen grains in water under a microscope. The specks were not alive, yet they never stopped zigzagging. Nobody could explain the shaking for the next 78 years.
cards.0.h: A gas is a crowd of particles
cards.0.p: Every cubic centimeter of the air in your room holds about 2.5·10¹⁹ particles. Even so, the gap between particles is about 10 times their own size. That empty space is why a gas squeezes easily and fills any container.
cards.0.key: A gas is a huge number of particles flying fast through mostly empty space.
cards.1.p: Kinetic theory is the model that explains a gas with moving particles. For an ideal gas it makes four assumptions. Particles move randomly in straight lines. Their own volume is negligible. They do not attract each other except during collisions. Collisions lose no kinetic energy.
cards.1.key: Ideal gas: particles with no volume, no attraction and elastic collisions.
cards.2.p: In 1905 Einstein explained why the pollen specks shake. Invisible water molecules hit the speck from every side, and at any moment the hits do not balance out. So the speck zigzags. In 1908 Jean Perrin measured this motion and showed that atoms are real.
cards.2.svg#1: invisible water molecules hit from every side
cards.2.key: Brownian motion is the visible trace of collisions with invisible particles.
cards.3.p: When a particle hits a wall head-on and bounces back at the same speed, its momentum changes by 2·m·v. The wall pushes on the particle, and the particle pushes back on the wall with an equal force. The average force of billions of hits per second on each unit of area is the gas pressure.
cards.3.key: Pressure = the average force per unit area from collisions.
cards.4.p: Pressure rises in two ways. Particles hit the walls either more often or harder. Shrinking the volume or adding gas makes hits more frequent. Heating the gas speeds the particles up, so the hits become both more frequent and harder.
cards.4.key: More frequent hits or faster particles mean higher pressure.
cards.5.p: Adding up the collisions gives P·V = ⅓·N·m·v². Here N is the number of particles and m is the mass of one particle. v² is the average of the squared particle speeds. So pressure grows with the square of particle speed.
cards.5.key: If the particles move twice as fast, the pressure becomes four times larger.
cards.6.p: Comparing this result with the ideal gas law gives the average kinetic energy of one particle: Ek = (3/2)·k·T. Here k = 1.38·10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant and T is in kelvin. Double the kelvin temperature and the average kinetic energy doubles too.
cards.6.key: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.
cards.7.h: The ideal gas law, particle by particle
cards.7.p: In chemistry the ideal gas law is written P·V = n·R·T. In physics the same law uses the number of particles: P·V = N·k·T. Both say the same thing, because R = NA·k: 6.02·10²³ × 1.38·10⁻²³ ≈ 8.31 J/(mol·K).
cards.7.key: n·R = N·k: count particles instead of moles.
cards.8.p: The square root of the average squared speed is the rms speed (vrms). You find it with vrms = √(3·R·T/M), where M is the molar mass in kg/mol. In air at 20 °C, nitrogen molecules travel about 510 meters every second.
cards.8.etk.soru: Change the temperature and the gas. Watch the rms speed of the particles.
cards.8.key: rms speed rises with the square root of temperature and falls with the square root of molar mass.
cards.9.h: Not all at the same speed
cards.9.p: Particles at the same temperature move at different speeds. The Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shows how those speeds are spread. When the gas warms up, the peak moves right and the curve spreads out. The very fast particles in the tail explain why water can evaporate without boiling.
cards.9.key: Temperature sets the average, while single particles have very different speeds.
cards.10.p: At the same temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy. So lighter particles must move faster. A hydrogen molecule is 4 times faster than an oxygen molecule. Light gases escape into space more easily, which is one reason Earth's air has so little free hydrogen.
cards.10.key: Same temperature means the same average energy, not the same speed.
cards.11.h: Why does a smell spread slowly?
cards.11.p: Particles travel hundreds of meters per second, but in air they move only about 70 nanometers between collisions. That distance is the mean free path. A particle changes direction billions of times every second. Without air currents, a smell would cross a room far more slowly.
cards.11.key: A fast particle that keeps colliding zigzags and makes slow progress.
cards.12.h: Internal energy of an ideal gas
cards.12.p: For a monatomic ideal gas, the internal energy is just the total kinetic energy of its particles: U = (3/2)·n·R·T. So the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature. Changing only pressure or volume leaves it the same. Thermodynamics starts from this idea.
cards.12.key: In an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature.
cards.13.p: At high pressure, the particles' own volume starts to matter. At low temperature, the attraction between particles becomes noticeable. In these two cases a gas moves away from the ideal model and can finally turn into a liquid. At room conditions, air behaves almost exactly like an ideal gas.
cards.13.key: The ideal model breaks down at high pressure and low temperature.
cards.14.p:
• A gas is made of particles moving randomly through mostly empty space.
• Pressure is the average force of collisions on the walls.
• Average kinetic energy is (3/2)·k·T and is proportional to kelvin temperature.
• rms speed is √(3·R·T/M), and lighter gases move faster.
• The ideal model breaks down at high pressure and low temperature.
quiz.0.q: The kelvin temperature of a gas in a sealed container doubles. What happens to the average kinetic energy of its particles?
quiz.0.e: Average kinetic energy is (3/2)·k·T. It is proportional to kelvin temperature, so it doubles too.
quiz.0.y.0: Heated particles speed up, they do not slow down.
quiz.0.y.1: Even in a sealed container, the particles gain energy from the heat.
quiz.0.y.3: It would quadruple if the speed doubled. Here the temperature is what doubles.
quiz.1.q: A gas at 300 K has an rms speed of 500 m/s. If it is heated to 1200 K, what is its rms speed in m/s?
quiz.1.e: rms speed grows with the square root of temperature. The temperature became 4 times larger, so the speed becomes √4 = 2 times larger: 1000 m/s.
quiz.2.q: With everything else held constant, which changes raise the pressure of a gas and which lower it?
quiz.2.e: Any change that makes collisions more frequent or particles faster raises the pressure. The opposite lowers it.
quiz.3.q: Match each idea with its description.
quiz.3.e: Brownian motion proves particles exist, pressure comes from collisions, temperature measures average kinetic energy, and the mean free path is the distance between collisions.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Squeeze the gas, heat it, add particles and see for yourself where pressure comes from.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A piston holds 1 mol of gas at 27 °C, 24.6 L and 1 atm. Watch the particles hit the walls. Find three different ways to double the pressure.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Reach 2 atm by changing only the volume.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: You halved the volume. The particles hit the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubled.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Reach 2 atm by changing only the temperature.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The temperature rose from 300 K to 600 K. The particles hit both more often and harder, and the pressure doubled.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Reach 2 atm by changing only the number of particles.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: With twice as many particles, there were twice as many collisions.
A:kapanis.0: Pressure comes from particles hitting the walls.
A:kapanis.1: Shrinking the volume or adding gas makes collisions more frequent.
A:kapanis.2: Heating speeds the particles up, so collisions become both more frequent and harder.
